questions.stem: State the lattice energy equation for sodium chloride with its value.
questions.modelAnswer: Na+ (g) plus Cl- (g) forming NaCl (s), delta latt H = -776 kJ mol^-1.

questions.stem: State the definition of the standard enthalpy change of atomisation.
questions.modelAnswer: The enthalpy change that accompanies 1 mole of gaseous atoms being produced from the element under standard conditions; always endothermic.

questions.stem: Explain why the more exothermic a lattice energy is, the stronger the ionic bonding.
questions.modelAnswer: A more negative lattice energy means more energy released when the ions assemble, which measures the depth of the electrostatic well between them; deeper wells take more energy to break, so the bonding is stronger.

questions.stem: Write the lattice energy equation for calcium chloride, noting how many chloride ions are involved.
questions.modelAnswer: Ca2+ (g) plus 2Cl- (g) forming CaCl2 (s), exothermic; two gaseous chloride ions combine with one calcium ion per formula unit, so any cycle doubles the chloride-side terms.

questions.stem: State the first electron affinity equation and value for chlorine.
questions.modelAnswer: Cl (g) plus e- forming Cl- (g), delta ea H = -364 kJ mol^-1.

questions.stem: State why second electron affinities are endothermic.
questions.modelAnswer: The incoming electron repels the already negative ion, and overcoming that repulsion requires energy input.

questions.stem: Explain why electron affinity belongs to the gaseous phase.
questions.modelAnswer: The definition isolates the atom-electron interaction from any lattice or solvent effects; only in the gas phase can the energy change of adding one electron to one atom be measured cleanly.

questions.stem: Predict the sign of the second electron affinity of nitrogen and justify in one sentence.
questions.modelAnswer: Endothermic: the electron must push past the repulsion of the already negative N- ion, so energy must be supplied.
